track.label: AWS From Scratch
track.headline: Build your own AWS
track.blurb: Learn about IAM, S3, leased queues, DynamoDB and more
track.description: Toy IAM, S3, SQS, DynamoDB, Lambda, SNS, KMS and VPC, plus a capstone that wires them and breaks them on purpose.
track.why: Eight mechanism families in pure Python, 18 checks. The best first course: no dependencies, every stage is a real failure mode.

stages_detail.title: explicit deny > allow > implicit deny
stages_detail.action: IAM: an explicit Deny wins; otherwise any matching Allow applies; otherwise implicit Deny.
stages_detail.why: This rule is what makes a policy SET composable: order never matters, so appending a guard policy can never break existing grants. Evaluate it like a firewall (first or last match wins) and the same policies behave differently depending on document order — no property you can reason about at scale.
stages_detail.predict: the result when Allow and Deny both match.

stages_detail.title: conditions: AND keys, OR values, fail closed
stages_detail.action: Policy conditions: AND across keys, OR within one key's values, and a MISSING context key never matches.
stages_detail.why: Fail-closed is not a style choice — it is the difference between a bug and a vulnerability. Treat an absent aws:SourceIp as 'any IP' and a request with no context at all bypasses every IP restriction. The AND/OR shape also returns in SNS filters (stage 16): learn it once here.
stages_detail.predict: a request with NO context keys against a policy requiring two conditions.

stages_detail.title: permissions boundaries subtract, never grant
stages_detail.action: Permissions boundaries: a boundary only SUBTRACTS from what identity policies grant, it can never grant.
stages_detail.why: If a boundary could grant, handing someone a boundary would be a privilege escalation, and delegation would be unsafe. Subtract-only is what makes 'you may be an admin of this project, never of IAM' expressible at all.
stages_detail.predict: Allow outside the boundary.

stages_detail.title: assume-role: caller policy AND role trust
stages_detail.action: Assume-role needs BOTH directions: the caller's own policy must allow sts:AssumeRole, AND the role's trust policy must allow that principal.
stages_detail.why: Two policies for two different attackers. Your own policy protects you from yourself (an intern's role-escape); the trust policy protects you from OTHER accounts — without it, anyone whose own policy says 'I may assume anything' walks into your roles.
stages_detail.predict: identity policy Allows but trust policy does not.

stages_detail.title: put/get objects and the NoSuchKey error
stages_detail.action: S3 objects: put/get with an ETag (the body's MD5), and a missing key raises NoSuchKey.
stages_detail.why: The ETag is the content hash because S3 is a flat KV store with no directories to hide consistency behind — the tag is your only cheap integrity check, and the NoSuchKey error (not a null) is how you distinguish 'absent' from 'present but empty'.
stages_detail.predict: what GET returns for a key that was never written.

stages_detail.title: multipart ETags end in -<part count>
stages_detail.action: Multipart ETags end in '-<part count>' and are NOT the object's MD5: parts assemble in order at complete().
stages_detail.why: A multipart ETag is the MD5 of the concatenated PART MD5s — hence the suffix. The practical consequence: you cannot verify a multipart upload by md5-ing your local file, and people burn hours on exactly that.
stages_detail.predict: the ETag of a two-part multipart upload.

stages_detail.title: delimiter invents folders at list time
stages_detail.action: Listing: without a delimiter every key returns flat; with delimiter='/', shared prefixes collapse into common_prefixes.
stages_detail.why: Folders do not exist in S3 — reports/2024/q1.csv is one opaque key. The delimiter INVENTS folders at list time, which is why an empty folder cannot exist and why 'renaming a folder' is O(every object under it).
stages_detail.predict: what list_objects returns for a/1.txt, a/2.txt, top.txt with delimiter='/'.

stages_detail.title: delete marker hides versions, frees nothing
stages_detail.action: In a versioned bucket, DELETE pushes a delete marker: plain GET then 404s, but every version is still stored — only deleting a version_id frees bytes.
stages_detail.why: Versioning makes buckets immutable-by-default, and DELETE must be undoable, so it appends instead of mutating. Consequence: 'I emptied the bucket' and 'the bill went down' are different claims — the bytes sit there, billable, under the marker.
stages_detail.predict: what GET returns after a delete marker is added.

stages_detail.title: receive is a lease; expiry redelivers
stages_detail.action: receive() is a LEASE, not a read: the visibility timeout hides a message; if it is not deleted in time it is redelivered.
stages_detail.why: Consumers crash mid-message, and the queue cannot know. A read must either lose the message or block the queue; a lease does neither. Redelivery is the queue CHOOSING duplication over loss — so your handler is idempotent or it is wrong.
stages_detail.predict: whether the same message is received twice.

stages_detail.title: stale receipt handles must fail to delete
stages_detail.action: Each receive gets its OWN receipt handle; after the lease expires, the FIRST consumer's delete must fail.
stages_detail.why: If both consumers shared one Message object, the second receive would overwrite the first's handle and the stale delete would silently succeed — deleting work someone else is still doing. Distinct handles make every delete prove its lease is current.
stages_detail.predict: whether consumer A's delete succeeds after B's redelivery.

stages_detail.title: change_visibility extends the lease
stages_detail.action: change_visibility extends a lease: a consumer whose work outlasts the timeout renews instead of racing redelivery.
stages_detail.why: Lease expiry exists for CRASHED consumers. A live slow consumer should never hit it — extending the deadline is the fix, and heartbeat loops in real systems are exactly this call on a timer.
stages_detail.predict: whether the message returns at the original timeout after an extension.

stages_detail.title: poison messages dead-letter after max_receives
stages_detail.action: Dead-letter queue: after max_receives the message moves to the DLQ instead of being delivered again.
stages_detail.why: Without a DLQ a poison message retries forever: it eats throughput AND hides every message behind it. Bounded retries plus a DLQ convert 'queue stuck' into 'queue moving, alarm on the DLQ depth'.
stages_detail.predict: how many times a failing message is delivered.

stages_detail.title: oldest_age counts in-flight messages too
stages_detail.action: oldest_age counts IN-FLIGHT messages too: a message being retried forever is old, not young.
stages_detail.why: The age alarm exists to catch the poison message — which spends most of its life in flight, invisible to a visible-only age. The metric must describe the queue's actual state, not the easy subset.
stages_detail.predict: oldest_age of a message received once and never deleted.

stages_detail.title: FIFO: one in-flight message per group
stages_detail.action: FIFO: only ONE in-flight message per message group; a different group is never blocked.
stages_detail.why: Ordering within a group is the entire point of groups — and it is exactly what forbids parallelism inside one. The group id is your concurrency dial: coarse enough to keep order, fine enough to keep throughput.
stages_detail.predict: how many of 3 same-group messages one receive returns.

stages_detail.title: FIFO dedup window drops duplicate ids
stages_detail.action: FIFO dedup: a duplicate dedup_id inside the 5-minute window is dropped; outside it is accepted again.
stages_detail.why: Producers retry on network flakiness; without dedup every retry is a duplicate order. A time window instead of forever keeps the dedup table bounded — the cost of the guarantee, and its expiry surprise.
stages_detail.predict: the second send with the same dedup_id at t=10 and at t=400.

stages_detail.title: composite key = partition + sort
stages_detail.action: DynamoDB composite key = partition + sort: get_item is keyed by BOTH, and query reads only one partition.
stages_detail.why: Keying by sort key alone would make alice/000 and bob/000 collide — silent data loss. And query's demand for the partition key is not a limitation, it is the CONTRACT that buys O(items returned) instead of O(table).
stages_detail.predict: whether Query can span partitions.

stages_detail.title: query reads one partition; missing key raises
stages_detail.action: Conditional writes: put with a condition raises ConditionalCheckFailed when it fails, and the failed write changes nothing.
stages_detail.why: The check and the write happen atomically inside one partition, which is how you get idempotent creates and optimistic locking with no lock service at all. Failing cleanly is the feature: it means someone got there first, exactly what you asked to know.
stages_detail.predict: the value after a failed conditional put.

stages_detail.title: conditional writes fail atomically
stages_detail.action: A strongly consistent read costs exactly TWICE an eventually consistent one.
stages_detail.why: Consistency is paid per read, not configured once: strong reads hit enough replicas to confirm, eventual ones hit one. Pricing it 2x is what makes people ask 'do I need consistent here?' instead of defaulting to yes.
stages_detail.predict: consistent cost for a 0.5-unit eventual read.

stages_detail.title: consistent reads cost twice eventual ones
stages_detail.action: Table capacity divides ACROSS partitions: 40 WCU on 4 partitions is 10 per partition, so 30 writes to ONE key throttle after 10 — with the table 75% idle.
stages_detail.why: Adding capacity does not help a hot key: the limit is per partition, and the key decides the partition. The fix is the data model (spread the key), not the bill — the most common DynamoDB surprise.
stages_detail.predict: how many of 30 same-key writes succeed (40 WCU, 4 partitions).

stages_detail.title: capacity divides across partitions; hot key throttles
stages_detail.action: Scan reads EVERY item and filters afterwards: a scan returning 3 of a million items costs a million reads.
stages_detail.why: Scan has no key to route by, so it walks every partition — you pay for what you read, not what you keep. Query, given the partition key, reads only what can match. That asymmetry is the whole data model.
stages_detail.predict: which costs more: query('alice') or scan(pk=='alice') on a 3-item table.

stages_detail.title: scan reads everything, then filters
stages_detail.action: Lambda cold start: the first invocation pays the init cost; warm invocations reuse the environment AND its memory.
stages_detail.why: The container outlives your invocation BY DESIGN — that is how init gets amortised. Consequence cut both ways: a connection pool is free, a cache you assumed empty is a correctness bug.
stages_detail.predict: how many inits over six invocations.

stages_detail.title: cold start once; warm state survives
stages_detail.action: An environment past its TTL is replaced (fresh state); a timeout is reported and billed in full.
stages_detail.why: Warm state is an optimisation, never a guarantee — AWS reclaims environments whenever it wants. Code that works only because the cache was warm is a bug with a timer on it. Timeouts bill fully because the capacity was truly occupied.
stages_detail.predict: the counter value after an invocation past the TTL.

stages_detail.title: environment TTL resets state; timeout bills full
stages_detail.action: Concurrency is a QUOTA, not a speed limit: 15 events against 10 shed 5. A reserved concurrency carves out capacity WHETHER USED OR NOT.
stages_detail.why: Reserving 6 of 10 for one function leaves 4 for every other function — they were never touched. The silent reduction of an unrelated function is the point: quotas are account-wide carpentry, not per-function dials.
stages_detail.predict: how many of 10 events the untouched function runs after the reservation.

stages_detail.title: concurrency is a quota; reservation steals a floor
stages_detail.action: Async failures retry to 3 total attempts, then the event lands in the dead-letter queue; sync failures return to the caller instead.
stages_detail.why: Same bug, different blast radius: sync surfaces the error to whoever can react; async retries blindly — so a non-idempotent handler runs THREE times: three charges, three emails.
stages_detail.predict: attempts for a failing async handler.

stages_detail.title: async failures retry to 3 attempts, then DLQ
stages_detail.action: SNS fans out: one publish delivers to EVERY subscriber — queues and Lambda handlers alike — on the same clock it was given.
stages_detail.why: Push means no consumer polls, so no buffering: SNS delivers and drops on failure, which is exactly why SNS → SQS → consumer is the standard shape rather than an accident. The clock threading is the bug that makes messages land 'in the future' in tests.
stages_detail.predict: queue depths right after a publish to 3 subscribers.

stages_detail.title: one publish fans out to every subscriber
stages_detail.action: Filter policies: AND across keys, OR within one, a MISSING attribute never matches, and no policy means deliver.
stages_detail.why: The same fail-closed rule as IAM conditions (stage 2): treating absent as permissive would silently route events that were supposed to be scoped. The filter runs at the TOPIC — drops happen before fanout, not at the consumer.
stages_detail.predict: which subscriptions a two-attribute message hits.

stages_detail.title: filters: AND keys, OR values, missing never matches
stages_detail.action: EventBridge matches the SHAPE of the event: patterns nest into detail, a key absent from the event cannot match, and one event fires EVERY matching rule.
stages_detail.why: Nothing deduplicates rule firing — two matching rules means double-processing, which is either free parallelism or a double-charge depending on whether you knew. Structural matching is what makes one bus carry every service's events.
stages_detail.predict: how many rules fire when one event matches two.

stages_detail.title: EventBridge matches nested shape, fires every rule
stages_detail.action: Envelope encryption: generate a data key (plaintext + wrapped copy), encrypt the data locally, store only the wrapped key alongside.
stages_detail.why: KMS is a vault with a 4KB door: you do not push data through it. The data never leaves you — size is unchanged — and KMS only ever touches the small key. That is the whole reason the payload limit never constrains you.
stages_detail.predict: what you must store alongside the ciphertext.

stages_detail.title: envelope: data key encrypts, CMK wraps the key
stages_detail.action: One KMS call per OBJECT, not per byte: encrypting 100KB uses one data key regardless of size.
stages_detail.why: The envelope inverts the cost model: KMS calls are the expensive, rate-limited part, local crypto is free. Per-byte KMS calls would be an outage; per-object is the pattern every encrypted store uses.
stages_detail.predict: data-key calls to encrypt 100KB.

stages_detail.title: one KMS call per object, not per byte
stages_detail.action: The encryption context must MATCH on decrypt — wrong, empty or missing context all fail.
stages_detail.why: The context is authenticated data: not secret, but bound into the unwrap. It is what lets an IAM condition scope a key to a tenant — decrypt refuses to run outside the context the key was created under.
stages_detail.predict: decrypt with a mismatched context.

stages_detail.title: encryption context must match on decrypt
stages_detail.action: Rotation creates a new key VERSION: new encryptions use it, old versions are retained, and ALL old ciphertext still decrypts. Deleting a version makes its ciphertext unrecoverable.
stages_detail.why: Re-encrypting all data on rotation would be an outage, so rotation re-encrypts KEYS, never DATA. The mandatory waiting period on deletion exists because 'unrecoverable' must be hard to do by accident.
stages_detail.predict: whether last year's ciphertext decrypts after rotation.

stages_detail.title: rotation re-encrypts keys, never data
stages_detail.action: CIDR: containment and overlap of subnets, and AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet — a /28 has 11 usable hosts, not 16.
stages_detail.why: The reserved five (network, DNS x2, broadcast, future) are the number people get wrong when sizing subnets — and overlapping subnets are rejected because routing must have exactly one answer for any address.
stages_detail.predict: usable hosts in a /28.

stages_detail.title: CIDR containment, overlap, 5 reserved IPs
stages_detail.action: Route tables match the LONGEST PREFIX, not the first or the shortest entry.
stages_detail.why: Most-specific wins is what lets a peering route (10.1.0.0/16) and a finer transit route (10.1.5.0/24) coexist with a default route — order in the table is irrelevant, exactly like IAM's deny-wins rule.
stages_detail.predict: which route wins for 10.0.1.5.

stages_detail.title: routes pick the longest matching prefix
stages_detail.action: Security groups are STATEFUL: allow the request in and the reply out is automatic. NACLs are STATELESS: same rules fail, because the reply goes to an EPHEMERAL port.
stages_detail.why: The reply is a new packet to 49152-65535, and nobody remembers to allow that. This is the single most common VPC bug, and it is invisible unless you model the whole connection — evaluate only the request and SG vs NACL look identical.
stages_detail.predict: why a NACL blocks the reply to an allowed request.

stages_detail.title: SG stateful vs NACL stateless, same rules
stages_detail.action: NACL rules evaluate in NUMBER order, first match wins: a deny at 100 shadows an allow at 200. Security groups have no deny — absence of an allow IS the deny.
stages_detail.why: Two more points on the same design axis: NACL buys explicit ordering (and pays with statelessness); SG buys simplicity (and cannot express deny). Neither is strictly better — they answer different questions.
stages_detail.predict: SSH from 10.0.5.5 against deny-100/allow-200 rules.

stages_detail.title: the pipeline, and failures surfacing a layer away
stages_detail.action: Capstone: wire S3 → SNS → SQS → Lambda → DynamoDB, KMS on the payload, IAM on every call — then watch a DynamoDB hot partition surface as a Lambda alarm.
stages_detail.why: Failures compose too: the cause lives in the data model, the alarm fires on compute, and the audit trail must record DENIED calls or you debug from half the evidence. That mismatch between where a failure is VISIBLE and where it is CAUSED is most of what makes distributed debugging hard.
stages_detail.predict: which service's failure stops the pipeline first.

track.label: Infrastructure
track.headline: Build your own Infrastructure
track.blurb: Learn about caching, rate limits, queues, capacity and more
track.description: The building blocks of distributed systems, one module each: consistent hashing, caching, CDN and rate limiting, batching, pooling, stickiness, circuit breaking, queues, leaderboards, hot partitions, locality, eventual consistency, idempotency, edge computing, capacity math.
track.why: Optional but cheap: caching, queues, idempotency, rate limiting. Makes sqs/dynamodb in A1 click and underpins the agent half. The graded course is `infrastructure-from-scratch/`: eighteen topic modules, each a stub whose own `_test()` describes the job, graded by `course.py` (surface + behaviour probe + the module's `_test()`), with anchored mutation batteries proving the grader catches planted mistakes — superseding the 6,000-line `system-design/` pile. The material still uses `time` and floats (TTLs and rate windows are wall-clock), so it does not conform to laws 2–3 of its contract; that debt is recorded there, not hidden.

stages_detail.title: URL shortener — base62 codes, TTL store, click stats
stages_detail.action: Implement base62 encode/decode, a URLStore with TTL expiry and hit stats, and a URLShortener that mints codes and resolves them.
stages_detail.predict: why must the code counter advance before encoding, never after?

stages_detail.title: Consistent hashing — virtual-node ring, rendezvous
stages_detail.action: Implement HashRing with virtual nodes (add/remove/get_node/distribution/migration_count) and RendezvousHash.
stages_detail.predict: adding one node to an N-node ring — how many keys move?

stages_detail.title: Cache — LRU, TTL, cache-aside, stampede protection
stages_detail.action: Implement LRUCache (dict + doubly-linked list, O(1) get/put), TTLCache, CacheAsideStore, and StampedeProtectedCache.
stages_detail.predict: can a get() be O(1) while keeping true recency order?

stages_detail.title: CDN — edge cache, origin shield, cache-key normalization
stages_detail.action: Implement EdgeCache honouring Cache-Control (private/no-store/max-age, surrogate keys, purge_by_key), OriginShield collapsing concurrent origin fetches, and normalize_cache_key.
stages_detail.predict: two objects sharing a surrogate key — how many does one purge remove?

stages_detail.title: Rate limiting — fixed window, token bucket, sliding window
stages_detail.action: Implement FixedWindow, TokenBucket (capacity + refill_rate), SlidingWindowLog and SlidingWindowCounter limiters.
stages_detail.predict: why does fixed window allow a 2× burst at the boundary?

stages_detail.title: Throttling — leaky bucket, delay throttle, worker drain
stages_detail.action: Implement LeakyBucket (capacity + drain_rate), DelayThrottler (minimum interval per key) and ThrottledWorker (rate-limited task pool).
stages_detail.predict: token bucket lets bursts through — which of these never does?

stages_detail.title: Request batching — size/time windows, DataLoader, pipeline
stages_detail.action: Implement SizeBatcher, TimeBatcher (window flush thread), DataLoader (dedupe same-window keys into one fetch) and PipelineBatcher.
stages_detail.predict: three threads ask for key 'user:1' in one window — how many fetches?

stages_detail.title: Connection pooling — acquire/release, exhaustion, idle eviction
stages_detail.action: Implement ConnectionPool (min/max size, acquire_timeout, idle_timeout eviction), PooledConnection as context manager, PoolExhaustedError naming the pool.
stages_detail.predict: why does acquire() wait on a condition instead of spinning?

stages_detail.title: Session stickiness — sticky routing, cookies, session store
stages_detail.action: Implement StickyRouter (hash → backend, health-aware), StickyLoadBalancer (SERVERID cookie affinity) and SessionStore (create/get/update/delete with TTL).
stages_detail.predict: a backend dies mid-session — what does the user lose, and when?

stages_detail.title: Circuit breaking — timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead
stages_detail.action: Implement with_timeout and retry decorators, the CLOSED→OPEN→HALF-OPEN CircuitBreaker, per-tenant Bulkhead semaphores, and BoundedQueue backpressure counting rejections.
stages_detail.predict: what must a half-open breaker do on its first success?

stages_detail.title: Message queue — retries, backoff, DLQ, idempotent delivery
stages_detail.action: Implement Message, MessageQueue (enqueue/dequeue/ack/nack with visibility, retry+backoff, dead-letter queue, idempotency-key dedup) and exponential_backoff(base, cap, jitter).
stages_detail.predict: nack with retries left — is the old message id ever seen again?

stages_detail.title: Leaderboards — sorted set, ranks, windows, rank delta
stages_detail.action: Implement SortedSet (zadd/zscore/zincrby/zrevrank/zrevrange/zrangebyscore/zcard), Leaderboard with snapshots and rank delta, and WindowedLeaderboard.
stages_detail.predict: why does a rank delta need a snapshot at all?

stages_detail.title: Hot partitions — scattered writes, hot-key detection, buckets
stages_detail.action: Implement ScatteredWriter (salted copies across N shards) with ScatterGatherReader, HotKeyDetector (sliding window counts), and TimeBucketedStore (bucketed range reads + aggregation).
stages_detail.predict: why scatter writes but not reads — what does a reader pay?

stages_detail.title: Data locality — shard routing, co-location, denormalized views
stages_detail.action: Implement ShardRouter (partition key → shard), CoLocationStore (related entities on one shard), DenormalizedOrderView (pre-joined writes fan out) and LocalityAwareCache.
stages_detail.predict: which read does denormalization make free — and which write it makes expensive?

stages_detail.title: Eventual consistency — CRDTs, vector clocks, read repair
stages_detail.action: Implement GCounter (merge by per-node max), LWWRegister (timestamp wins), VectorClock with happened_before, Replica, and EventuallyConsistentStore with quorum writes and read repair.
stages_detail.predict: two replicas tick their own clock — is either's write before the other's?

stages_detail.title: Idempotency keys — dedup store, single execution, payments
stages_detail.action: Implement IdempotencyStore (get_or_create/complete, TTL, purge_expired), IdempotentHandler (concurrent callers → exactly one execution), and PaymentProcessor (idempotent charges).
stages_detail.predict: five threads POST the same charge key — how many debits happen?

stages_detail.title: Edge computing — latency routing, middleware, A/B, runtime
stages_detail.action: Implement LatencyRouter (nearest healthy PoP), EdgeMiddlewarePipeline (auth/geo chain), ABTestRouter (deterministic hashed buckets) and EdgeRuntime (per-function CPU limit, EdgeFunctionError naming the offender).
stages_detail.predict: why must the A/B bucket hash the user id, not the request?

stages_detail.title: Capacity planning — QPS, storage, bandwidth, server estimates
stages_detail.action: Implement compute_qps (DAU × actions → average + peak), compute_storage (write QPS × payload × replication per day), compute_bandwidth, cache_impact, estimate_servers (Little's Law) and the human_bytes/human_num formatters.
stages_detail.predict: cache hit ratio goes up 10% — what happens to DB QPS?

track.label: LLM From Scratch
track.headline: Build your own LLM
track.blurb: Learn about tokenization, attention, sampling, KV cache and more
track.description: The forward-pass mechanisms of a language model in plain Python (BPE, attention, sampling, the KV cache, RoPE), the modern architectures built on them (MoE, GQA, MLA, SSMs, diffusion, TTT, Titans, MoD), and the distributed-training machinery (tensor/ZeRO/pipeline/expert parallelism, mixed precision, FlashAttention, checkpointing).
track.why: BPE, attention, sampling, KV cache, RoPE. 13 checks, pure Python.

stages_detail.title: pair counts and non-overlapping merges
stages_detail.action: Write get_pair_counts as a dict of adjacent pairs, then merge_pair with an index that SKIPS PAST each merge, so [1,1,1] becomes [9,1] and not two overlapping merges.
stages_detail.predict: In [1,1,1,2], how many adjacent (1,1) pairs? (two, not three)

stages_detail.title: deterministic training and compression
stages_detail.action: In train_bpe, take the most frequent pair but break ties by the smallest pair, and start new ids at 256. Determinism is the whole point — same corpus, same table.
stages_detail.predict: Train twice on one corpus: identical merge table?

stages_detail.title: rank-ordered encode and round-trip
stages_detail.action: Make encode repeatedly apply the LOWEST-RANK merge anywhere in the sequence (not a left-to-right sweep); decode expands ids bottom-up.

stages_detail.title: stable softmax
stages_detail.action: In softmax, subtract the row max before exp: exp(x - max). The result is identical and can never overflow.
stages_detail.predict: softmax([1000,1001]) — finite, and sums to 1.

stages_detail.title: attention weights and the causal mask
stages_detail.action: Apply the causal mask as -inf BEFORE the softmax, so each row still sums to 1 and position 0 attends only to itself.
stages_detail.predict: the output row for position 0 equals V[0].

stages_detail.title: temperature and hard greedy
stages_detail.action: temperature 0 is hard greedy: one-hot at the argmax, -inf everywhere else. Temperature divides the logits.
stages_detail.predict: sample(temp=0) is deterministic — the tail can never fire.

stages_detail.title: top-k
stages_detail.action: top_k keeps the k largest and breaks ties by smallest index, keeping BOTH tied values.
stages_detail.predict: top-2 of [1,3,3,2] keeps indices 1 and 2.

stages_detail.title: top-p keeps the crossing token
stages_detail.action: top_p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, INCLUDING the token that crosses it (>= not >).
stages_detail.predict: [.5,.3,.15,.05] at p=.9 keeps the .15 token.

stages_detail.title: seeded sampling is reproducible
stages_detail.action: Thread the Random instance you were handed through every sampling call; never touch the global random module.
stages_detail.predict: one seed twice gives the same 50 samples.

stages_detail.title: cache append and shape
stages_detail.action: KVCache stores parallel key/value lists; append, and make len/keys/values reflect exactly what was appended.
stages_detail.predict: the length after two appends.

stages_detail.title: cached output is bit-exact
stages_detail.action: cached_step must reproduce recompute_step to <1e-9: append the new K/V and attend over ALL cached rows — read the cache.
stages_detail.predict: dropping the last key must change the output.

stages_detail.title: the cost model: linear vs quadratic
stages_detail.action: Count interactions: recompute is O(t*d) per step (quadratic overall), the cache is O(d) plus the append (linear).
stages_detail.predict: doubling the prompt multiplies prefill work by ~4.

stages_detail.title: norm and relative-position invariants
stages_detail.action: Rotate each (x2i, x2i+1) pair by pos*freq; check the norm is preserved and dot(q@p, k@p+d) ignores p entirely.
stages_detail.predict: the relative dot product is identical for every p.

stages_detail.title: MoE: routing and expert loads
stages_detail.action: Router logits are dot products; route to the top_k experts by score (ties by lower index) and renormalise over the CHOSEN ones only.
stages_detail.predict: top-2 of scores [1.0, 0.2, 1.08] picks experts 2 and 0.

stages_detail.title: GQA: shared KV heads
stages_detail.action: Group KV heads into contiguous groups; each query head maps to KV head h % n_kv, cycling when there are more query heads.
stages_detail.predict: 32 query heads, 8 KV heads: the cache is a quarter the size.

stages_detail.title: MLA: latent compression
stages_detail.action: Compress with an orthonormal seeded matrix (y = Wx), decompress with its transpose (x' = W^T y). W^T W = I makes the full-size roundtrip exact; a small latent must lose information.
stages_detail.predict: the roundtrip error with latent = full dim (must be ~0).

stages_detail.title: SSM: selective recurrence
stages_detail.action: h' = exp(delta*A)*h + delta*B*x, y = C·h'. delta is the input-dependent gate: exp(delta*A) compounds every step.
stages_detail.predict: an impulse with delta=1, A=-1 decays: 1, e^-1, e^-2...

stages_detail.title: diffusion: mask and denoise
stages_detail.action: Mask with the handed Random instance only; denoise unmasks the keep most-confident MASKED positions — already-final tokens are ignored.
stages_detail.predict: rounds to fully unmask 10 tokens keeping 4/round (round up).

stages_detail.title: TTT: inner-loop learning
stages_detail.action: One gradient step on (target - w·x)^2: w' = w + 2*lr*err*x. Train in sequence order; later tokens overwrite earlier ones.
stages_detail.predict: error on the FIRST token after training the whole sequence (substantial).

stages_detail.title: Titans: neural memory
stages_detail.action: m' = m + lr*(surprise*x + momentum*prev_update), then 10% weight decay. Momentum carries the previous update through the window.
stages_detail.predict: how many trailing tokens still influence the memory (the window).

stages_detail.title: MoD: routed capacity
stages_detail.action: Pick exactly capacity positions by score (ties by lower index); every other row PASSES THROUGH UNCHANGED — that is the FLOP saving.
stages_detail.predict: the multiply-adds skipped: (rows - capacity) * d.

stages_detail.title: tensor parallelism
stages_detail.action: Column shards hold all rows / a band of columns and CONCATENATE; row shards hold a band of rows / all columns and ALL-REDUCE.
stages_detail.predict: which path needs the all-reduce (row-parallel).

stages_detail.title: ZeRO model-state sharding
stages_detail.action: Adam holds 4 floats per param (w, g, m, v). ZeRO partitions: stage 1 the optimizer state, 2 + gradients, 3 + parameters.
stages_detail.predict: ZeRO-3 across 4 workers: exactly a quarter of the full footprint.

stages_detail.title: GPipe microbatching
stages_detail.action: Stage s starts microbatch t-s at step t (the staircase). Bubble = (stages-1) / (stages-1 + microbatches) — more microbatches shrink it.
stages_detail.predict: the bubble fraction for 4 stages, 8 microbatches (3/11).

stages_detail.title: mixed precision
stages_detail.action: fp16 rounds to even at halfway (1+2^-11 stays 1.0; 1+2^-10+2^-11 steps up). Grads are fp16-rounded; the update lands on fp32 masters.
stages_detail.predict: summing 60000+60000 in fp16 (overflow at 65504).

stages_detail.title: FlashAttention tiling
stages_detail.action: Fold tiles with a running max: rescale the accumulator by exp(old_max - new_max) each time. Never materialise the t*t scores.
stages_detail.predict: tiled vs naive output difference (~0 to 1e-9).

stages_detail.title: activation checkpointing
stages_detail.action: Keep a checkpoint every k blocks, then RECOMPUTE the rest segment by segment. The recomputed activations must match eager exactly.
stages_detail.predict: stored + one-block-recompute vs every-block (the saving).

stages_detail.title: sequence parallelism
stages_detail.action: Scatter the sequence into shards, reduce partial sums of x and x^2 across workers, then normalise. Must match single-worker LayerNorm.
stages_detail.predict: sequence-parallel vs local LayerNorm difference (~0).

stages_detail.title: context parallelism
stages_detail.action: The query positions are FIXED across ring steps; only the KV shard moves. Mask by absolute position, fold with the running max.
stages_detail.predict: query 0's denominator after every shard (only key 0 is unmasked).

stages_detail.title: expert parallelism
stages_detail.action: Expert e lives on worker e % n_workers; dispatch groups token indices by their expert's worker, the combine scatters them back.
stages_detail.predict: tokens [0,1,2,0] with experts [0,1,2,0] on 2 workers: [[0,2,3],[1]].

items.title: AWS From Scratch
items.why: Eight mechanism families in pure Python, 18 checks. The best first course: no dependencies, every stage is a real failure mode.

stages.title: explicit deny > allow > implicit deny
stages.action: IAM: an explicit Deny wins; otherwise any matching Allow applies; otherwise implicit Deny.
stages.why: This rule is what makes a policy SET composable: order never matters, so appending a guard policy can never break existing grants. Evaluate it like a firewall (first or last match wins) and the same policies behave differently depending on document order — no property you can reason about at scale.
stages.predict: the result when Allow and Deny both match.

stages.title: conditions: AND keys, OR values, fail closed
stages.action: Policy conditions: AND across keys, OR within one key's values, and a MISSING context key never matches.
stages.why: Fail-closed is not a style choice — it is the difference between a bug and a vulnerability. Treat an absent aws:SourceIp as 'any IP' and a request with no context at all bypasses every IP restriction. The AND/OR shape also returns in SNS filters (stage 16): learn it once here.
stages.predict: a request with NO context keys against a policy requiring two conditions.

stages.title: permissions boundaries subtract, never grant
stages.action: Permissions boundaries: a boundary only SUBTRACTS from what identity policies grant, it can never grant.
stages.why: If a boundary could grant, handing someone a boundary would be a privilege escalation, and delegation would be unsafe. Subtract-only is what makes 'you may be an admin of this project, never of IAM' expressible at all.
stages.predict: Allow outside the boundary.

stages.title: assume-role: caller policy AND role trust
stages.action: Assume-role needs BOTH directions: the caller's own policy must allow sts:AssumeRole, AND the role's trust policy must allow that principal.
stages.why: Two policies for two different attackers. Your own policy protects you from yourself (an intern's role-escape); the trust policy protects you from OTHER accounts — without it, anyone whose own policy says 'I may assume anything' walks into your roles.
stages.predict: identity policy Allows but trust policy does not.

stages.title: put/get objects and the NoSuchKey error
stages.action: S3 objects: put/get with an ETag (the body's MD5), and a missing key raises NoSuchKey.
stages.why: The ETag is the content hash because S3 is a flat KV store with no directories to hide consistency behind — the tag is your only cheap integrity check, and the NoSuchKey error (not a null) is how you distinguish 'absent' from 'present but empty'.
stages.predict: what GET returns for a key that was never written.

stages.title: multipart ETags end in -<part count>
stages.action: Multipart ETags end in '-<part count>' and are NOT the object's MD5: parts assemble in order at complete().
stages.why: A multipart ETag is the MD5 of the concatenated PART MD5s — hence the suffix. The practical consequence: you cannot verify a multipart upload by md5-ing your local file, and people burn hours on exactly that.
stages.predict: the ETag of a two-part multipart upload.

stages.title: delimiter invents folders at list time
stages.action: Listing: without a delimiter every key returns flat; with delimiter='/', shared prefixes collapse into common_prefixes.
stages.why: Folders do not exist in S3 — reports/2024/q1.csv is one opaque key. The delimiter INVENTS folders at list time, which is why an empty folder cannot exist and why 'renaming a folder' is O(every object under it).
stages.predict: what list_objects returns for a/1.txt, a/2.txt, top.txt with delimiter='/'.

stages.title: delete marker hides versions, frees nothing
stages.action: In a versioned bucket, DELETE pushes a delete marker: plain GET then 404s, but every version is still stored — only deleting a version_id frees bytes.
stages.why: Versioning makes buckets immutable-by-default, and DELETE must be undoable, so it appends instead of mutating. Consequence: 'I emptied the bucket' and 'the bill went down' are different claims — the bytes sit there, billable, under the marker.
stages.predict: what GET returns after a delete marker is added.

stages.title: receive is a lease; expiry redelivers
stages.action: receive() is a LEASE, not a read: the visibility timeout hides a message; if it is not deleted in time it is redelivered.
stages.why: Consumers crash mid-message, and the queue cannot know. A read must either lose the message or block the queue; a lease does neither. Redelivery is the queue CHOOSING duplication over loss — so your handler is idempotent or it is wrong.
stages.predict: whether the same message is received twice.

stages.title: stale receipt handles must fail to delete
stages.action: Each receive gets its OWN receipt handle; after the lease expires, the FIRST consumer's delete must fail.
stages.why: If both consumers shared one Message object, the second receive would overwrite the first's handle and the stale delete would silently succeed — deleting work someone else is still doing. Distinct handles make every delete prove its lease is current.
stages.predict: whether consumer A's delete succeeds after B's redelivery.

stages.title: change_visibility extends the lease
stages.action: change_visibility extends a lease: a consumer whose work outlasts the timeout renews instead of racing redelivery.
stages.why: Lease expiry exists for CRASHED consumers. A live slow consumer should never hit it — extending the deadline is the fix, and heartbeat loops in real systems are exactly this call on a timer.
stages.predict: whether the message returns at the original timeout after an extension.

stages.title: poison messages dead-letter after max_receives
stages.action: Dead-letter queue: after max_receives the message moves to the DLQ instead of being delivered again.
stages.why: Without a DLQ a poison message retries forever: it eats throughput AND hides every message behind it. Bounded retries plus a DLQ convert 'queue stuck' into 'queue moving, alarm on the DLQ depth'.
stages.predict: how many times a failing message is delivered.

stages.title: oldest_age counts in-flight messages too
stages.action: oldest_age counts IN-FLIGHT messages too: a message being retried forever is old, not young.
stages.why: The age alarm exists to catch the poison message — which spends most of its life in flight, invisible to a visible-only age. The metric must describe the queue's actual state, not the easy subset.
stages.predict: oldest_age of a message received once and never deleted.

stages.title: FIFO: one in-flight message per group
stages.action: FIFO: only ONE in-flight message per message group; a different group is never blocked.
stages.why: Ordering within a group is the entire point of groups — and it is exactly what forbids parallelism inside one. The group id is your concurrency dial: coarse enough to keep order, fine enough to keep throughput.
stages.predict: how many of 3 same-group messages one receive returns.

stages.title: FIFO dedup window drops duplicate ids
stages.action: FIFO dedup: a duplicate dedup_id inside the 5-minute window is dropped; outside it is accepted again.
stages.why: Producers retry on network flakiness; without dedup every retry is a duplicate order. A time window instead of forever keeps the dedup table bounded — the cost of the guarantee, and its expiry surprise.
stages.predict: the second send with the same dedup_id at t=10 and at t=400.

stages.title: composite key = partition + sort
stages.action: DynamoDB composite key = partition + sort: get_item is keyed by BOTH, and query reads only one partition.
stages.why: Keying by sort key alone would make alice/000 and bob/000 collide — silent data loss. And query's demand for the partition key is not a limitation, it is the CONTRACT that buys O(items returned) instead of O(table).
stages.predict: whether Query can span partitions.

stages.title: query reads one partition; missing key raises
stages.action: Conditional writes: put with a condition raises ConditionalCheckFailed when it fails, and the failed write changes nothing.
stages.why: The check and the write happen atomically inside one partition, which is how you get idempotent creates and optimistic locking with no lock service at all. Failing cleanly is the feature: it means someone got there first, exactly what you asked to know.
stages.predict: the value after a failed conditional put.

stages.title: conditional writes fail atomically
stages.action: A strongly consistent read costs exactly TWICE an eventually consistent one.
stages.why: Consistency is paid per read, not configured once: strong reads hit enough replicas to confirm, eventual ones hit one. Pricing it 2x is what makes people ask 'do I need consistent here?' instead of defaulting to yes.
stages.predict: consistent cost for a 0.5-unit eventual read.

stages.title: consistent reads cost twice eventual ones
stages.action: Table capacity divides ACROSS partitions: 40 WCU on 4 partitions is 10 per partition, so 30 writes to ONE key throttle after 10 — with the table 75% idle.
stages.why: Adding capacity does not help a hot key: the limit is per partition, and the key decides the partition. The fix is the data model (spread the key), not the bill — the most common DynamoDB surprise.
stages.predict: how many of 30 same-key writes succeed (40 WCU, 4 partitions).

stages.title: capacity divides across partitions; hot key throttles
stages.action: Scan reads EVERY item and filters afterwards: a scan returning 3 of a million items costs a million reads.
stages.why: Scan has no key to route by, so it walks every partition — you pay for what you read, not what you keep. Query, given the partition key, reads only what can match. That asymmetry is the whole data model.
stages.predict: which costs more: query('alice') or scan(pk=='alice') on a 3-item table.

stages.title: scan reads everything, then filters
stages.action: Lambda cold start: the first invocation pays the init cost; warm invocations reuse the environment AND its memory.
stages.why: The container outlives your invocation BY DESIGN — that is how init gets amortised. Consequence cut both ways: a connection pool is free, a cache you assumed empty is a correctness bug.
stages.predict: how many inits over six invocations.

stages.title: cold start once; warm state survives
stages.action: An environment past its TTL is replaced (fresh state); a timeout is reported and billed in full.
stages.why: Warm state is an optimisation, never a guarantee — AWS reclaims environments whenever it wants. Code that works only because the cache was warm is a bug with a timer on it. Timeouts bill fully because the capacity was truly occupied.
stages.predict: the counter value after an invocation past the TTL.

stages.title: environment TTL resets state; timeout bills full
stages.action: Concurrency is a QUOTA, not a speed limit: 15 events against 10 shed 5. A reserved concurrency carves out capacity WHETHER USED OR NOT.
stages.why: Reserving 6 of 10 for one function leaves 4 for every other function — they were never touched. The silent reduction of an unrelated function is the point: quotas are account-wide carpentry, not per-function dials.
stages.predict: how many of 10 events the untouched function runs after the reservation.

stages.title: concurrency is a quota; reservation steals a floor
stages.action: Async failures retry to 3 total attempts, then the event lands in the dead-letter queue; sync failures return to the caller instead.
stages.why: Same bug, different blast radius: sync surfaces the error to whoever can react; async retries blindly — so a non-idempotent handler runs THREE times: three charges, three emails.
stages.predict: attempts for a failing async handler.

stages.title: async failures retry to 3 attempts, then DLQ
stages.action: SNS fans out: one publish delivers to EVERY subscriber — queues and Lambda handlers alike — on the same clock it was given.
stages.why: Push means no consumer polls, so no buffering: SNS delivers and drops on failure, which is exactly why SNS → SQS → consumer is the standard shape rather than an accident. The clock threading is the bug that makes messages land 'in the future' in tests.
stages.predict: queue depths right after a publish to 3 subscribers.

stages.title: one publish fans out to every subscriber
stages.action: Filter policies: AND across keys, OR within one, a MISSING attribute never matches, and no policy means deliver.
stages.why: The same fail-closed rule as IAM conditions (stage 2): treating absent as permissive would silently route events that were supposed to be scoped. The filter runs at the TOPIC — drops happen before fanout, not at the consumer.
stages.predict: which subscriptions a two-attribute message hits.

stages.title: filters: AND keys, OR values, missing never matches
stages.action: EventBridge matches the SHAPE of the event: patterns nest into detail, a key absent from the event cannot match, and one event fires EVERY matching rule.
stages.why: Nothing deduplicates rule firing — two matching rules means double-processing, which is either free parallelism or a double-charge depending on whether you knew. Structural matching is what makes one bus carry every service's events.
stages.predict: how many rules fire when one event matches two.

stages.title: EventBridge matches nested shape, fires every rule
stages.action: Envelope encryption: generate a data key (plaintext + wrapped copy), encrypt the data locally, store only the wrapped key alongside.
stages.why: KMS is a vault with a 4KB door: you do not push data through it. The data never leaves you — size is unchanged — and KMS only ever touches the small key. That is the whole reason the payload limit never constrains you.
stages.predict: what you must store alongside the ciphertext.

stages.title: envelope: data key encrypts, CMK wraps the key
stages.action: One KMS call per OBJECT, not per byte: encrypting 100KB uses one data key regardless of size.
stages.why: The envelope inverts the cost model: KMS calls are the expensive, rate-limited part, local crypto is free. Per-byte KMS calls would be an outage; per-object is the pattern every encrypted store uses.
stages.predict: data-key calls to encrypt 100KB.

stages.title: one KMS call per object, not per byte
stages.action: The encryption context must MATCH on decrypt — wrong, empty or missing context all fail.
stages.why: The context is authenticated data: not secret, but bound into the unwrap. It is what lets an IAM condition scope a key to a tenant — decrypt refuses to run outside the context the key was created under.
stages.predict: decrypt with a mismatched context.

stages.title: encryption context must match on decrypt
stages.action: Rotation creates a new key VERSION: new encryptions use it, old versions are retained, and ALL old ciphertext still decrypts. Deleting a version makes its ciphertext unrecoverable.
stages.why: Re-encrypting all data on rotation would be an outage, so rotation re-encrypts KEYS, never DATA. The mandatory waiting period on deletion exists because 'unrecoverable' must be hard to do by accident.
stages.predict: whether last year's ciphertext decrypts after rotation.

stages.title: rotation re-encrypts keys, never data
stages.action: CIDR: containment and overlap of subnets, and AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet — a /28 has 11 usable hosts, not 16.
stages.why: The reserved five (network, DNS x2, broadcast, future) are the number people get wrong when sizing subnets — and overlapping subnets are rejected because routing must have exactly one answer for any address.
stages.predict: usable hosts in a /28.

stages.title: CIDR containment, overlap, 5 reserved IPs
stages.action: Route tables match the LONGEST PREFIX, not the first or the shortest entry.
stages.why: Most-specific wins is what lets a peering route (10.1.0.0/16) and a finer transit route (10.1.5.0/24) coexist with a default route — order in the table is irrelevant, exactly like IAM's deny-wins rule.
stages.predict: which route wins for 10.0.1.5.

stages.title: routes pick the longest matching prefix
stages.action: Security groups are STATEFUL: allow the request in and the reply out is automatic. NACLs are STATELESS: same rules fail, because the reply goes to an EPHEMERAL port.
stages.why: The reply is a new packet to 49152-65535, and nobody remembers to allow that. This is the single most common VPC bug, and it is invisible unless you model the whole connection — evaluate only the request and SG vs NACL look identical.
stages.predict: why a NACL blocks the reply to an allowed request.

stages.title: SG stateful vs NACL stateless, same rules
stages.action: NACL rules evaluate in NUMBER order, first match wins: a deny at 100 shadows an allow at 200. Security groups have no deny — absence of an allow IS the deny.
stages.why: Two more points on the same design axis: NACL buys explicit ordering (and pays with statelessness); SG buys simplicity (and cannot express deny). Neither is strictly better — they answer different questions.
stages.predict: SSH from 10.0.5.5 against deny-100/allow-200 rules.

stages.title: the pipeline, and failures surfacing a layer away
stages.action: Capstone: wire S3 → SNS → SQS → Lambda → DynamoDB, KMS on the payload, IAM on every call — then watch a DynamoDB hot partition surface as a Lambda alarm.
stages.why: Failures compose too: the cause lives in the data model, the alarm fires on compute, and the audit trail must record DENIED calls or you debug from half the evidence. That mismatch between where a failure is VISIBLE and where it is CAUSED is most of what makes distributed debugging hard.
stages.predict: which service's failure stops the pipeline first.

items.title: LLM From Scratch
items.why: BPE, attention, sampling, KV cache, RoPE. 13 checks, pure Python.

stages.title: pair counts and non-overlapping merges
stages.action: Write get_pair_counts as a dict of adjacent pairs, then merge_pair with an index that SKIPS PAST each merge, so [1,1,1] becomes [9,1] and not two overlapping merges.
stages.predict: In [1,1,1,2], how many adjacent (1,1) pairs? (two, not three)

stages.title: deterministic training and compression
stages.action: In train_bpe, take the most frequent pair but break ties by the smallest pair, and start new ids at 256. Determinism is the whole point — same corpus, same table.
stages.predict: Train twice on one corpus: identical merge table?

stages.title: rank-ordered encode and round-trip
stages.action: Make encode repeatedly apply the LOWEST-RANK merge anywhere in the sequence (not a left-to-right sweep); decode expands ids bottom-up.

stages.title: stable softmax
stages.action: In softmax, subtract the row max before exp: exp(x - max). The result is identical and can never overflow.
stages.predict: softmax([1000,1001]) — finite, and sums to 1.

stages.title: attention weights and the causal mask
stages.action: Apply the causal mask as -inf BEFORE the softmax, so each row still sums to 1 and position 0 attends only to itself.
stages.predict: the output row for position 0 equals V[0].

stages.title: temperature and hard greedy
stages.action: temperature 0 is hard greedy: one-hot at the argmax, -inf everywhere else. Temperature divides the logits.
stages.predict: sample(temp=0) is deterministic — the tail can never fire.

stages.title: top-k
stages.action: top_k keeps the k largest and breaks ties by smallest index, keeping BOTH tied values.
stages.predict: top-2 of [1,3,3,2] keeps indices 1 and 2.

stages.title: top-p keeps the crossing token
stages.action: top_p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, INCLUDING the token that crosses it (>= not >).
stages.predict: [.5,.3,.15,.05] at p=.9 keeps the .15 token.

stages.title: seeded sampling is reproducible
stages.action: Thread the Random instance you were handed through every sampling call; never touch the global random module.
stages.predict: one seed twice gives the same 50 samples.

stages.title: cache append and shape
stages.action: KVCache stores parallel key/value lists; append, and make len/keys/values reflect exactly what was appended.
stages.predict: the length after two appends.

stages.title: cached output is bit-exact
stages.action: cached_step must reproduce recompute_step to <1e-9: append the new K/V and attend over ALL cached rows — read the cache.
stages.predict: dropping the last key must change the output.

stages.title: the cost model: linear vs quadratic
stages.action: Count interactions: recompute is O(t*d) per step (quadratic overall), the cache is O(d) plus the append (linear).
stages.predict: doubling the prompt multiplies prefill work by ~4.

stages.title: norm and relative-position invariants
stages.action: Rotate each (x2i, x2i+1) pair by pos*freq; check the norm is preserved and dot(q@p, k@p+d) ignores p entirely.
stages.predict: the relative dot product is identical for every p.

stages.title: MoE: routing and expert loads
stages.action: Router logits are dot products; route to the top_k experts by score (ties by lower index) and renormalise over the CHOSEN ones only.
stages.predict: top-2 of scores [1.0, 0.2, 1.08] picks experts 2 and 0.

stages.title: GQA: shared KV heads
stages.action: Group KV heads into contiguous groups; each query head maps to KV head h % n_kv, cycling when there are more query heads.
stages.predict: 32 query heads, 8 KV heads: the cache is a quarter the size.

stages.title: MLA: latent compression
stages.action: Compress with an orthonormal seeded matrix (y = Wx), decompress with its transpose (x' = W^T y). W^T W = I makes the full-size roundtrip exact; a small latent must lose information.
stages.predict: the roundtrip error with latent = full dim (must be ~0).

stages.title: SSM: selective recurrence
stages.action: h' = exp(delta*A)*h + delta*B*x, y = C·h'. delta is the input-dependent gate: exp(delta*A) compounds every step.
stages.predict: an impulse with delta=1, A=-1 decays: 1, e^-1, e^-2...

stages.title: diffusion: mask and denoise
stages.action: Mask with the handed Random instance only; denoise unmasks the keep most-confident MASKED positions — already-final tokens are ignored.
stages.predict: rounds to fully unmask 10 tokens keeping 4/round (round up).

stages.title: TTT: inner-loop learning
stages.action: One gradient step on (target - w·x)^2: w' = w + 2*lr*err*x. Train in sequence order; later tokens overwrite earlier ones.
stages.predict: error on the FIRST token after training the whole sequence (substantial).

stages.title: Titans: neural memory
stages.action: m' = m + lr*(surprise*x + momentum*prev_update), then 10% weight decay. Momentum carries the previous update through the window.
stages.predict: how many trailing tokens still influence the memory (the window).

stages.title: MoD: routed capacity
stages.action: Pick exactly capacity positions by score (ties by lower index); every other row PASSES THROUGH UNCHANGED — that is the FLOP saving.
stages.predict: the multiply-adds skipped: (rows - capacity) * d.

stages.title: tensor parallelism
stages.action: Column shards hold all rows / a band of columns and CONCATENATE; row shards hold a band of rows / all columns and ALL-REDUCE.
stages.predict: which path needs the all-reduce (row-parallel).

stages.title: ZeRO model-state sharding
stages.action: Adam holds 4 floats per param (w, g, m, v). ZeRO partitions: stage 1 the optimizer state, 2 + gradients, 3 + parameters.
stages.predict: ZeRO-3 across 4 workers: exactly a quarter of the full footprint.

stages.title: GPipe microbatching
stages.action: Stage s starts microbatch t-s at step t (the staircase). Bubble = (stages-1) / (stages-1 + microbatches) — more microbatches shrink it.
stages.predict: the bubble fraction for 4 stages, 8 microbatches (3/11).

stages.title: mixed precision
stages.action: fp16 rounds to even at halfway (1+2^-11 stays 1.0; 1+2^-10+2^-11 steps up). Grads are fp16-rounded; the update lands on fp32 masters.
stages.predict: summing 60000+60000 in fp16 (overflow at 65504).

stages.title: FlashAttention tiling
stages.action: Fold tiles with a running max: rescale the accumulator by exp(old_max - new_max) each time. Never materialise the t*t scores.
stages.predict: tiled vs naive output difference (~0 to 1e-9).

stages.title: activation checkpointing
stages.action: Keep a checkpoint every k blocks, then RECOMPUTE the rest segment by segment. The recomputed activations must match eager exactly.
stages.predict: stored + one-block-recompute vs every-block (the saving).

stages.title: sequence parallelism
stages.action: Scatter the sequence into shards, reduce partial sums of x and x^2 across workers, then normalise. Must match single-worker LayerNorm.
stages.predict: sequence-parallel vs local LayerNorm difference (~0).

stages.title: context parallelism
stages.action: The query positions are FIXED across ring steps; only the KV shard moves. Mask by absolute position, fold with the running max.
stages.predict: query 0's denominator after every shard (only key 0 is unmasked).

stages.title: expert parallelism
stages.action: Expert e lives on worker e % n_workers; dispatch groups token indices by their expert's worker, the combine scatters them back.
stages.predict: tokens [0,1,2,0] with experts [0,1,2,0] on 2 workers: [[0,2,3],[1]].

items.title: Context Caching From Scratch
items.why: The direct continuation of A2: page, prefix-share, evict the KV cache without changing the output. 16 checks.

stages.title: linear algebra helpers
stages.action: Implement the plain-list vector helpers (dot, softmax, matmul) first — everything above is built from them.
stages.predict: the shape of a 2x3 times 3x2 result.

stages.title: KVCache append/truncate/clone
stages.action: append/truncate/clone must keep keys and values aligned; clone must deep-copy rows, not share them.
stages.predict: mutating a clone leaves the original untouched.

stages.title: cached == uncached attention
stages.action: Cached attention must equal uncached attention within tolerance — append the new K/V and attend over all rows.
stages.predict: the max difference between cached and uncached.

stages.title: prefill and the cost model
stages.action: Prefill is quadratic in prompt length; decode is linear. Count multiply-adds to make the difference concrete.
stages.predict: the ratio of prefill work at 128 vs 64 tokens.

stages.title: layer_norm and gelu
stages.action: layer_norm needs a variance epsilon; gelu uses the tanh approximation. Match the checker's tolerance exactly.
stages.predict: layer_norm of a constant vector.

stages.title: generation matches exactly
stages.action: Generation with the cache must be token-identical to the no-cache path — same logits, same argmax.
stages.predict: the generated token sequence with and without cache.

stages.title: truncate, clone, prefix reuse
stages.action: truncate must cut keys and values together; clone must not share rows; prefix reuse must not mutate the source request.
stages.predict: reusing a prefix twice gives the same continuation.

stages.title: block hashing and chaining
stages.action: Hash each token block, then CHAIN: the child's hash includes the parent's, so identical prefixes share one key.
stages.predict: do two prompts sharing a prefix produce one shared block?

stages.title: matching, eviction, isolation
stages.action: Match the longest cached prefix, evict by policy, and keep per-request isolation — one request must not evict another's pinned blocks.
stages.predict: the hit length for a prompt sharing 2 of 3 blocks.

stages.title: matching and node splitting
stages.action: Radix matching walks edge labels and SPLITS a node when a prefix ends mid-edge — test the split explicitly.
stages.predict: the tree shape after inserting 'abc' then 'abd'.

stages.title: eviction and pinning
stages.action: Evict leaves first; pinned nodes are exempt. Walk to find a valid victim rather than evicting the root.
stages.predict: which node is evicted when all are leaves.

stages.title: block allocation and growth
stages.action: The block allocator hands out fixed-size blocks and grows the block table; track free/used and refcounts.
stages.predict: how many blocks a 17-token sequence with block=8 needs.

stages.title: forking and copy-on-write
stages.action: fork shares blocks by reference (refcount++); a WRITE to a shared block copies it first (refcount--, new block).
stages.predict: does writing to a fork change the parent's tokens?

stages.title: exact and semantic caching
stages.action: Exact cache first, then a semantic threshold — tune it so near-duplicates hit but distinct prompts miss.
stages.predict: whether a reworded question should be a hit.

stages.title: cache-aware routing
stages.action: Route each request to the replica that already holds its prefix; fall back to least-loaded when nobody does.
stages.predict: the hit rate after routing vs round-robin.

stages.title: capstone: identical output
stages.action: Capstone: wire prefix + paged + semantic caches together and keep the output identical to the uncached model.
stages.predict: compute saved (%) and whether output is bit-identical.

items.title: ContextCite From Scratch
items.why: Which context caused the answer — ablation and a LASSO surrogate. The eval-flavoured course, and the bridge into RAG. 14 checks.

stages.title: splitting text into sources
stages.action: Split text into sources with offsets precise enough to rebuild the full context byte-for-byte.
stages.predict: the number of sources in a 3-sentence passage.

stages.title: rebuilding ablated contexts
stages.action: Rebuild the ablated context from a kept-source mask, preserving order and spacing exactly.
stages.predict: the context when only source 2 is kept.

stages.title: logit-prob math and stability
stages.action: logit-prob = logit[target] - logsumexp(logits); subtract the max inside logsumexp so it never overflows.
stages.predict: log-prob of a token with logit 0 among [0,0,0].

stages.title: aggregation and response score
stages.action: Aggregate per-token logit-probs into one response score — pick sum or mean and apply it consistently.
stages.predict: sum vs mean on a 4-token response.

stages.title: sampling the design matrix
stages.action: Sample a binary design matrix over sources; each row is a kept/dropped subset of the context.
stages.predict: how many distinct rows a 5-source sampler can produce.

stages.title: soft threshold and standardising
stages.action: Coordinate-descent LASSO: soft-threshold each coordinate and standardise inputs so the penalty is comparable across sources.
stages.predict: soft_threshold(0.5, 1.0).

stages.title: recovering a known sparse signal
stages.action: Fit should recover a known sparse signal — check the support and the coefficient signs against ground truth.
stages.predict: which coefficients are exactly zero.

stages.title: end-to-end attribution
stages.action: End-to-end: abduction (drop sources) -> design matrix -> LASSO -> per-source attribution scores.
stages.predict: the coefficient on the source the answer actually needs.

stages.title: span attribution, zero extra calls
stages.action: Span attribution reuses the same ablation samples — assert the number of model calls does NOT grow with span count.
stages.predict: model calls with 1 source vs 4 spans.

stages.title: spearman rank correlation
stages.action: Spearman: rank both vectors and correlate the ranks; assign average ranks on ties.
stages.predict: Spearman of a perfectly reversed ranking.

stages.title: held-out LDS and top-k drop
stages.action: Held-out LDS and top-k drop: measure whether the surrogate predicts on ablations it never saw.
stages.predict: LDS of a perfect ranker.

stages.title: verification and pruning
stages.action: Applications: verify a claim by ablation, and prune sources the surrogate calls dead.
stages.predict: whether removing the top source flips the answer.

stages.title: detecting a poisoned source
stages.action: Detect a poisoned source: its coefficient should dominate, and no honest source should be a perfect predictor.
stages.predict: the coefficient profile with one injected source.

stages.title: leave-one-out fails on redundancy
stages.action: Leave-one-out fails under redundancy — two identical sources split the credit and each looks unimportant. Reproduce it.
stages.predict: each duplicate's leave-one-out score.

items.title: System Design
items.why: Optional but cheap: caching, queues, idempotency, rate limiting. Makes sqs/dynamodb in A1 click and underpins the agent half. The graded course is `infrastructure-from-scratch/`: eighteen topic modules, each a stub whose own `_test()` describes the job, graded by `course.py` (surface + behaviour probe + the module's `_test()`), with anchored mutation batteries proving the grader catches planted mistakes — superseding the 6,000-line `system-design/` pile. The material still uses `time` and floats (TTLs and rate windows are wall-clock), so it does not conform to laws 2–3 of its contract; that debt is recorded there, not hidden.

stages.title: URL shortener — base62 codes, TTL store, click stats
stages.action: Implement base62 encode/decode, a URLStore with TTL expiry and hit stats, and a URLShortener that mints codes and resolves them.
stages.predict: why must the code counter advance before encoding, never after?

stages.title: Consistent hashing — virtual-node ring, rendezvous
stages.action: Implement HashRing with virtual nodes (add/remove/get_node/distribution/migration_count) and RendezvousHash.
stages.predict: adding one node to an N-node ring — how many keys move?

stages.title: Cache — LRU, TTL, cache-aside, stampede protection
stages.action: Implement LRUCache (dict + doubly-linked list, O(1) get/put), TTLCache, CacheAsideStore, and StampedeProtectedCache.
stages.predict: can a get() be O(1) while keeping true recency order?

stages.title: CDN — edge cache, origin shield, cache-key normalization
stages.action: Implement EdgeCache honouring Cache-Control (private/no-store/max-age, surrogate keys, purge_by_key), OriginShield collapsing concurrent origin fetches, and normalize_cache_key.
stages.predict: two objects sharing a surrogate key — how many does one purge remove?

stages.title: Rate limiting — fixed window, token bucket, sliding window
stages.action: Implement FixedWindow, TokenBucket (capacity + refill_rate), SlidingWindowLog and SlidingWindowCounter limiters.
stages.predict: why does fixed window allow a 2× burst at the boundary?

stages.title: Throttling — leaky bucket, delay throttle, worker drain
stages.action: Implement LeakyBucket (capacity + drain_rate), DelayThrottler (minimum interval per key) and ThrottledWorker (rate-limited task pool).
stages.predict: token bucket lets bursts through — which of these never does?

stages.title: Request batching — size/time windows, DataLoader, pipeline
stages.action: Implement SizeBatcher, TimeBatcher (window flush thread), DataLoader (dedupe same-window keys into one fetch) and PipelineBatcher.
stages.predict: three threads ask for key 'user:1' in one window — how many fetches?

stages.title: Connection pooling — acquire/release, exhaustion, idle eviction
stages.action: Implement ConnectionPool (min/max size, acquire_timeout, idle_timeout eviction), PooledConnection as context manager, PoolExhaustedError naming the pool.
stages.predict: why does acquire() wait on a condition instead of spinning?

stages.title: Session stickiness — sticky routing, cookies, session store
stages.action: Implement StickyRouter (hash → backend, health-aware), StickyLoadBalancer (SERVERID cookie affinity) and SessionStore (create/get/update/delete with TTL).
stages.predict: a backend dies mid-session — what does the user lose, and when?

stages.title: Circuit breaking — timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead
stages.action: Implement with_timeout and retry decorators, the CLOSED→OPEN→HALF-OPEN CircuitBreaker, per-tenant Bulkhead semaphores, and BoundedQueue backpressure counting rejections.
stages.predict: what must a half-open breaker do on its first success?

stages.title: Message queue — retries, backoff, DLQ, idempotent delivery
stages.action: Implement Message, MessageQueue (enqueue/dequeue/ack/nack with visibility, retry+backoff, dead-letter queue, idempotency-key dedup) and exponential_backoff(base, cap, jitter).
stages.predict: nack with retries left — is the old message id ever seen again?

stages.title: Leaderboards — sorted set, ranks, windows, rank delta
stages.action: Implement SortedSet (zadd/zscore/zincrby/zrevrank/zrevrange/zrangebyscore/zcard), Leaderboard with snapshots and rank delta, and WindowedLeaderboard.
stages.predict: why does a rank delta need a snapshot at all?

stages.title: Hot partitions — scattered writes, hot-key detection, buckets
stages.action: Implement ScatteredWriter (salted copies across N shards) with ScatterGatherReader, HotKeyDetector (sliding window counts), and TimeBucketedStore (bucketed range reads + aggregation).
stages.predict: why scatter writes but not reads — what does a reader pay?

stages.title: Data locality — shard routing, co-location, denormalized views
stages.action: Implement ShardRouter (partition key → shard), CoLocationStore (related entities on one shard), DenormalizedOrderView (pre-joined writes fan out) and LocalityAwareCache.
stages.predict: which read does denormalization make free — and which write it makes expensive?

stages.title: Eventual consistency — CRDTs, vector clocks, read repair
stages.action: Implement GCounter (merge by per-node max), LWWRegister (timestamp wins), VectorClock with happened_before, Replica, and EventuallyConsistentStore with quorum writes and read repair.
stages.predict: two replicas tick their own clock — is either's write before the other's?

stages.title: Idempotency keys — dedup store, single execution, payments
stages.action: Implement IdempotencyStore (get_or_create/complete, TTL, purge_expired), IdempotentHandler (concurrent callers → exactly one execution), and PaymentProcessor (idempotent charges).
stages.predict: five threads POST the same charge key — how many debits happen?

stages.title: Edge computing — latency routing, middleware, A/B, runtime
stages.action: Implement LatencyRouter (nearest healthy PoP), EdgeMiddlewarePipeline (auth/geo chain), ABTestRouter (deterministic hashed buckets) and EdgeRuntime (per-function CPU limit, EdgeFunctionError naming the offender).
stages.predict: why must the A/B bucket hash the user id, not the request?

stages.title: Capacity planning — QPS, storage, bandwidth, server estimates
stages.action: Implement compute_qps (DAU × actions → average + peak), compute_storage (write QPS × payload × replication per day), compute_bandwidth, cache_impact, estimate_servers (Little's Law) and the human_bytes/human_num formatters.
stages.predict: cache hit ratio goes up 10% — what happens to DB QPS?

items.title: Dynamo From Scratch
items.why: The paper behind DynamoDB, in depth: quorums, hinted handoff, Merkle anti-entropy. 17 checks.

stages.title: ring: add/remove/coordinator
stages.action: Ring: place a node's tokens, find a key's successor clockwise, and remove the node's tokens when it leaves.
stages.predict: who coordinates a key between two nodes.

stages.title: preference lists (N distinct nodes)
stages.action: preference_list walks virtual tokens clockwise and must SKIP nodes already chosen, returning N DISTINCT nodes.
stages.predict: N when the ring has fewer than N nodes.

stages.title: load balance and key migration
stages.action: Adding/removing a node should move about 1/N of the keys; measure balance as max/min load across nodes.
stages.predict: the fraction of keys that move when one node joins.

stages.title: strategy 3: fixed partitions
stages.action: Strategy 3: fixed partitions (a fixed Q), each node owns several — routing is a table lookup, not a ring walk.
stages.predict: how key movement compares to the ring.

stages.title: clock ordering and merge
stages.action: Vector clocks compare pointwise: equal, descendant, ancestor, or concurrent — get all four cases right.
stages.predict: the relation between {A:1} and {A:1,B:1}.

stages.title: reconciliation (paper Figure 3)
stages.action: On conflicting siblings, reconcile with the paper's rule and MERGE the clocks so the result dominates both.
stages.predict: the merged clock of two concurrent writes.

stages.title: clock truncation
stages.action: Truncate the clock by dropping the oldest entries when it exceeds the cap, keeping recent causality.
stages.predict: which entries survive a cap of 2.

stages.title: storage node keeps siblings
stages.action: A storage node keeps the value plus all its siblings; a read returns every sibling, not just the newest.
stages.predict: the sibling count after two concurrent writes.

stages.title: N/R/W put and get
stages.action: N/R/W put and get: write to N preference nodes, read from R, and R+W>N is what guarantees overlap.
stages.predict: whether R=1,W=1,N=3 can read a stale value.

stages.title: siblings and read repair
stages.action: Reads collect siblings from R nodes; read repair pushes the newest value back to the stale replicas it saw.
stages.predict: which replicas get repaired on a read.

stages.title: sloppy quorum writes a hint
stages.action: Sloppy quorum: when a preference node is down, write to the next live node and store a HINT saying where it belongs.
stages.predict: hint count after one node is down.

stages.title: hinted handoff delivery
stages.action: Deliver hints when the owner returns, then delete the local copy — delivery must be idempotent.
stages.predict: what happens if the same hint is delivered twice.

stages.title: merkle tree build and diff
stages.action: Merkle tree: hash leaves (key ranges), hash pairs upward; the diff walks only branches whose hashes differ.
stages.predict: how many nodes one changed key dirties.

stages.title: anti-entropy is a union
stages.action: Anti-entropy is a UNION of values, reconciled with the same clock logic — not blind last-write-wins.
stages.predict: the value after syncing two divergent replicas.

stages.title: gossip convergence O(log S)
stages.action: Gossip converges in O(log S): each round every node tells a few peers; track rounds to full knowledge.
stages.predict: rounds for 64 nodes to all learn one fact.

stages.title: local failure detection, seeds
stages.action: Failure detection is local (heartbeat + suspicion), and seeds are how a brand-new node joins without a full member list.
stages.predict: how a node is declared dead with no central registry.

stages.title: capstone: cart + availability
stages.action: Capstone: run the cart workload against the full cluster and hit the stated availability target.
stages.predict: successful-write rate under 30% node churn.

items.title: Deploy & Debug
items.why: Capacity math, SLOs, root-causing faults from metrics. The operations thread that every later course leans on. 12 checks.

stages.title: KV cache and batch-size math
stages.action: KV cache bytes/token = 2 * layers * KV_HEADS * head_dim * bytes. Using query heads sizes the fleet 4x too large.
stages.predict: bytes/token for Llama-3-8B (8 KV heads).

stages.title: fleet sizing and quorum tolerance
stages.action: Size the fleet from concurrency and tokens/s, then subtract the failure tolerance R+W>N implies.
stages.predict: how many nodes can die and quorum still hold.

stages.title: percentiles and summaries
stages.action: Percentiles are not averages: sort and take the rank. p99 is where the outliers live.

stages.title: queueing and fan-out tails
stages.action: Little's law and fan-out: one slow dependency multiplies the tail across parallel calls.
stages.predict: tail latency with 10 parallel 100ms calls.

stages.title: SLOs, budgets and burn rate
stages.action: SLO is an objective over a window; error budget = 1 - SLO; burn rate is how fast you are spending it.
stages.predict: the error budget for 99.9% over 30 days.

stages.title: diagnose 6 serving faults
stages.action: Map each fault to its metric signature: KV full -> cache-miss spike; overload -> queue growth.
stages.predict: the signature of a full KV cache.

stages.title: undersized KV vs overload
stages.action: Undersized KV and overload look similar — separate them by cache-hit rate and memory, not latency alone.
